title: Exposure to corruption and individual well-being: A randomized controlled trial
abstract: Objectives This study examines the effect of corruption on well-being and tests three potential mediators: generalized trust, institutional trust, and locus of control. Methods We conducted a randomized controlled experiment with 837 United Kingdom citizens in which perceived exposure to corruption was manipulated. Structural equation modeling was used to assess the direct effect of corruption on two dimensions of well-being – positive affect and life satisfaction – as well as its indirect effects through the three potential mediators. Results Corruption had no significant direct effect on either positive affect or life satisfaction, but was indirectly associated with both outcomes through generalized trust. In contrast, institutional trust and locus of control did not emerge as significant mediators. Conclusions The findings suggest that corruption undermines individual well-being by eroding trust in fellow citizens and weakening the social fabric on which individual well-being depends.
